requirement: Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents reviewing code against requirements to inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling, and verify both that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and that it introduces no additional end-user-observable behavior without an agreed requirement. Where requirements interact, agents MUST cite every applicable requirement at the relevant implementation point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone MUST NOT count as that explanation.
rationale: All three bundled skills direct agents to inspect every end-user-observable result and branch against the applicable requirement texts, identify unspecified behavior, cite every interacting requirement, and explain the mapping beyond the presence of a tag.

text: Review every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Verify that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and does not introduce additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite all of them at meaningful implementation points and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. For example, a `^C` shortcut needs a requirement that explains why it is accepted. A tag alone does not establish that the behavior matches the requirement. Use the bundled `habeas-requirements` and `habeas-evidence` guidance for directive syntax and evidence records. Each evidence record must cite exact current lines covering every reference to its definition. Judge each requirement or example from the code and test results; a tag alone does not justify `determination: true`.

When checking a determination against code, inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Confirm that the code does what each applicable requirement says and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite every applicable requirement at the relevant implementation point and explain in the rationale how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone does not prove the behavior is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference, including trait methods and test helpers. Each example cites a requirement. Do not waive an uncited function because it is an internal helper. If no behavior-specific requirement explains it, propose an explicit project requirement such as `internal-detail` for the user's agreement, cite it, and give evidence for each such function explaining why it introduces no additional end-user-observable behavior. Do not use internal-detail to justify unspecified observable behavior.

Inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Check that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, cite every applicable requirement at the relevant implementation point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone does not explain why a behavior, such as accepting `^C`, is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference in an attached Rust comment or within its body, including trait methods and test helpers. Each example cites a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions, and there is no uncited-function waiver. If no existing requirement explains an internal helper, propose a project requirement such as `internal-detail` for the user's agreement, cite it on the function, and record evidence explaining why each such function adds no end-user-observable behavior beyond the requirements it supports. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior.
